In April 1241 two Mongol armies crushed Poland and Hungary within two days. A year later they were gone from Central Europe. The map of 1250 shows what stayed behind.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ The campaign began in the east. The Mongols sacked Ryazan in December 1237 and Kiev on 6 December 1240. The huge block on the right is the Golden Horde, the western khanate led by Batu Khan, a grandson of Genghis.

2/ On 9 April 1241 one army defeated a Polish-Moravian force under Henry II the Pious at Legnica. Two days later the main army routed King Béla IV of Hungary at Mohi on the Sajó river. Hungary's royal army was almost wiped out.
3/ Estimates of Hungary's losses range from about 20-40% of the population to as much as half, through killing and the disease that followed.

4/ Then, in 1242, they left. The usual explanation is the death of Great Khan Ögedei on 11 December 1241, which pulled the princes home. Some historians argue that stone fortifications and strained siege resources mattered more.
5/ Hungary drew the lesson. Béla IV pushed a wave of stone castle building, and when Nogai Khan raided Hungary again in 1285 the outcome was very different.

6/ Elsewhere on the map: on 5 April 1242 Alexander Nevsky beat the Livonian Order on frozen Lake Peipus, and in the south the Empire of Nicaea was a few years away from retaking Constantinople in 1261.
Ögedei's death or Europe's castles: what really stopped the Mongols? Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
